title: Guide
text: What using Docket commits a project to: how the project is structured, and how its work moves through Feature Promotion Flow. It states the method as the development standards Docket is built to state it.

flow.title: Feature Promotion Flow
flow.text: A project's record is its use cases, stories, scenarios, work items and decisions, kept as files in the repository on a branch of their own. Every feature lives on its own branch, cut from that record. Features are merged into `development` to be tested together. A release is assembled on `stage` from the features chosen for it, verified, and promoted to `main`. The record travels with the code the whole way, so a build carries its own work items.

sections.title: What using Docket commits a project to
sections.html:
What using Docket commits a project to

Using Docket commits a project to two things: it is structured as this part describes, and its work moves through Feature Promotion Flow, which the rest of this guide describes.

The two go together. Docket keeps the project's record as files in the project's own repository, on a branch of its own, and it reads where each work item stands from the merges in the history. So it shows where work stands only for work that moved as the flow says.

Every step is plain Git. A project on Docket can be worked on without Docket, and nothing here makes that impossible.

sections.title: What Docket keeps
sections.html:
What Docket keeps

Docket keeps what is to be built and what was done about it: use cases, stories, scenarios, work items and decisions, and the record of the work done on them, which is the estimates, the attempts and the test runs.

  • The backlog is the ledger

    Past, present and future work. Each item carries its status and its notes, and bringing the ledger forward to main with every release is the goal. A record kept apart from the code is not this design.

  • Docket writes files and does not commit

    A person or an agent commits what it wrote.

  • The record is these folders

    .docket/ holds the use cases, stories, work items, decisions and the record of the work. features/ holds the scenarios, in feature files. docs/ and the Markdown files at the top of the project are record too, so documentation is changed where the record is.

  • It lives on one branch

    docket-record, permanent and never reset, with no code committed on it. The only branch ever merged into it is main. It is checked out in a folder of its own, which is the folder Docket is served from, and each feature is worked on in a folder of its own, on a branch named from its work item. Why the record has its own branch is in Part 2; what each branch holds, and where everyone works, are in Part 3.

sections.title: A project with no docket-record branch
sections.html:
A project with no docket-record branch

A project on Docket has a docket-record branch. Where a copy of the project has none, it may only be missing from that copy: fetch first.

If the Git host has none either, the project's adoption of Docket is unfinished, or its .docket/ folder is a leftover. Say so, and stop before writing any record: no work is cut, and the branch is not created in passing. Creating it is part of adopting Docket.

sections.title: Why it exists, and why the record has its own branch
sections.html:
Why it exists

Most branching methods tie two decisions together: testing a feature with the others, and releasing it. Where features are cut from a shared development branch and merged back into it, whatever is on that branch is in the next release unless someone backs it out. One unfinished feature holds up everything behind it.

Feature Promotion Flow separates the two. A feature is merged into development to be tested with the others, and that says nothing about release. The release is assembled separately, on stage, from the features chosen for it, each merged from its own branch.

It is close to the method the Git project uses to build Git itself, gitworkflow: topic branches that graduate through integration branches, and tagged releases. In the projects it was written for, it replaced gitflow.

Why the record has its own branch

Docket is the program that keeps the record and shows it to people and to agents. A project on Docket keeps its record as files in the repository: use cases, stories, scenarios, work items and decisions, with the attempts and test runs made on them. The method needs that record in two places at once: where the work is planned, and inside every feature built from it.

Written on a feature, a work item would not reach main, or any other feature, until that feature was released. Kept in a branch that never meets the code, it would stop being part of the codebase, and a work item could no longer be tied to a build and carried along with it.

So the record has one permanent branch, docket-record: main plus everything recorded since. It holds the released code, and no code is committed on it, so it never holds unreleased code. Every feature is cut from it, so a feature holds its own work item and scenarios from its first commit. Because it holds no unreleased code, cutting from it brings no other feature along, which is what lets a release be chosen feature by feature.

What it gives you

  • A release is chosen, not inherited

    Being on development does not put a feature in a release. The maintainer, the person who decides what is released, chooses the set feature by feature.

  • Development may be broken

    It is where features are tried together. A break is fixed on the feature's own branch, and it does not hold up the release of the others.

  • Many features at once

    Every feature is built to stand alone, so several people or agents can build at the same time, each in a folder of its own (a Git worktree).

  • What is verified is what ships

    stage holds the release set, verified as a whole. The one merge made after QA brings the record, with QA's result and the acceptance, and a check confirms that nothing but the record changed since the commit QA tested.

  • A failed feature comes out cleanly

    Usually stage is rebuilt without it. Nothing is backed out, and nothing is patched in place.

  • A release carries its own proof

    QA's result and the maintainer's acceptance are recorded and travel to main with the release they belong to.

  • A hotfix takes a release's road, alone

    Recorded, cut from the record, verified on stage, promoted. It does not pass through development first, and it never goes straight to main.

  • The history says where work has been

    Every merge is a real merge whose title names both branches, so Git can say which branches hold a feature.

  • Plain Git

    Every step is ordinary Git, with pull requests on GitHub, and can be done by hand. Docket writes the record; the code can be worked on without it.

sections.title: Its limits, stated first
sections.html:
1

Its limits, stated first

What has and has not been shown, what the method costs, what it leaves out, and how it compares with the most common alternative.

  • The evidence so far

    The method is new. As it is written here it has been run on one project, through few releases. Nothing here has yet been shown with several people on several machines, and every benefit below should be read with that in mind.

  • What it costs

    A release of n features is 2n + 3 pull requests: each feature into development and into stage, the record into stage, stage into main, and the record into development. It is also n code reviews, a candidate built and tested on a machine, and one full QA run. A feature that fails on stage usually costs a reset, the candidate built again, a pull request for each feature that remains, and QA again. A hotfix is four pull requests, a code review and a QA run, and sets aside any release being assembled.

  • What it does not cover

    The method says nothing about database migrations, or about fixing an older version while a newer one is out: there is one released line. It does not say how a release is deployed, and its rollback (see the section on a bad release) assumes the previous release can be deployed again.

  • Against trunk-based development

    Trunk-based development with feature flags separates testing from releasing another way: everything merges to one branch daily, and a flag decides what is released. It integrates sooner and needs no assembly. It asks that unfinished work be safe to ship switched off, and the flags, not the history, say what a release contains. This method makes the other trade. Integration comes later and costs more pull requests. In return a release is a set of whole features, each with its own record, tests and code review, and what is left out is not in the build at all.

Designed in, and not yet proven by use

  • Release documents read out of the record

    The data is in the record. Docket does not yet produce release notes from it.

  • Fewer regressions

    This is what the design should produce. Too few releases have been through stage to show it.

  • Reliable release dates

    They depend on features staying independent. Where features require each other, a coordination handles it, at the cost of some freedom to choose.

sections.title: Where Docket keeps your tickets
sections.html:
2

Where Docket keeps your tickets

Docket is a ticket tracker. It has a backlog, statuses, an order, and people assigned to work. You write a ticket before the work starts, update it as the work moves, and look at it to see where things stand. If you have used a tracker before, you know how to use this one.

One thing is different. The tickets are files in your repository, not rows in a database on someone else's server. They travel with the code, so they are available to both the AI and the humans.

In the rest of this guide a ticket is called a work item, and the tickets with everything kept beside them are called the record.

What that gives you

  • Anyone with the code has the tracker

    A person or an agent who clones the repository has every ticket, with no second login and no integration.

  • A feature's branch carries its own ticket

    The scenarios it has to meet and the results of testing it sit beside the code that was built against them.

  • A release carries its tickets as they stood

    Check out last year's release and you can read what was asked for and what was accepted.

  • A change to a ticket is a commit

    Who changed it, when, and what it said before are in the history, like any other file.

  • The acceptance criteria are the files the tests run

    The ticket and the tests cannot say different things.

Where the tickets are kept

The tickets are kept on a branch of their own, docket-record. It gives you three things.

  • A place to write tickets to

    A ticket can be added or changed at any time, whatever state the code is in.

  • A place as recent as production

    After every release, docket-record takes in what was released, so it never lags behind what is live.

  • A place everyone can reach without conflicts

    People and agents all read and write tickets there, and no one's ticket change collides with someone else's code.

Docket runs on your machine and shows you the files on docket-record as pages, and you change a ticket through it. Committing that change is still yours to do.

If you work by hand

You can use all of this without Docket, because docket-record is the tracker.

  • To look at a ticket

    Pull docket-record and read the file.

  • To change a ticket

    Edit the file on docket-record, commit, and push.

  • To start work

    Cut your branch from docket-record and not from main, so the work begins with its own ticket.

  • Before your work moves on

    Pull docket-record into your branch, so the ticket and its results go with it.

sections.title: What the parts add up to
sections.html:
3

What the parts add up to

Each of these comes from two or more pieces of the method working together, which is why no single rule delivers it.

  • One record, open to everyone who works on it

    The record is files in the repository, so a person and an agent read and write the same work items, scenarios and decisions from the same checkout. Anyone with the repository needs no separate login, connector or export to see what the work is, and every feature branch carries the record it was built from.

  • Reliable release dates

    A release is chosen from what is ready, so the date does not wait on one unfinished feature. stage is rebuilt and not patched, so a late failure removes one feature, not the release. The date is the promise; the contents are whatever is ready by then.

  • Fewer regressions

    Scenarios are written before the branch exists, so behaviour is pinned down first. The whole suite runs on the exact combination that ships. And after a hotfix the record carries the fix into development, so the next release cannot quietly lose it.

  • Release documents read out of the record

    A release is a known list of work items, each with its story, scenarios, test results and decisions. Release notes, a change log, a notice to users and an audit trail are the same data read out in different forms.

  • Coordination without status meetings

    The backlog is the ledger. What is in progress, what could ship, what is blocked and on what are questions the record answers. Work items name what they wait for, and a coordination (see features that require each other) ties features that require each other.

  • Accountability across people and agents

    Every commit names the person, the agent and the model. Decisions are kept in the words of whoever made them. Checking is done by someone who did not build. An agent's work is as open to inspection as a person's.

  • Continuity

    A new person or a fresh agent reads the record and knows why things are as they are. Nothing depends on who remembers.

Fixed places to test, and to record the result

sections.title: Problems teams commonly report, and what this does about them
sections.html:
4

Problems teams commonly report, and what this does about them

Complaints teams commonly voice, with what this method does about each.

The complaintWhat this method does
“One unfinished feature is blocking the release.”A release is assembled from chosen features. The unfinished one stays on development.
“We need a code freeze before every release.”development never freezes. The release is built on stage, apart from ongoing work.
“Merge hell on long-lived branches.”Features are built to be independent, and conflicts surface on development early. A conflict resolved once can be replayed by Git's recorded resolutions (rerere), on the machine that resolved it.
“The hotfix never made it back, and the bug returned.”A hotfix takes the same road, and development gets the fix from the record straight after.
“It worked in testing but not in the release.”The code QA verifies on stage is the code promoted: only the record is merged after QA, and that is checked. Before that, the set is tested together as a candidate, and stage is checked against it, tree against tree.
“We reverted it and now the history is a mess.”Before promotion nothing is reverted: stage is rebuilt without the feature. A bad release already on main is put back by deploying the previous release again, then corrected by a hotfix. main is never reverted.
“Nobody knows what is actually in this release.”The release is a list of work items in the record, and the history names every branch merged and the pull request that merged it.
“Release notes are a scramble.”They can be read out of the release's work items. Docket does not produce them yet.
“The tracker and the code disagree.”The tracker is in the repository and moves with the code.
“Half the team, and all of the agents, cannot see the tickets.”The record is files in the repository. Anyone with the code has the work items, the scenarios and the decisions.
“Why was this decision made?”Decisions are recorded with the work, in the words of whoever made them.
“QA is a rubber stamp, or the author tested their own work.”QA is done by a fresh agent that has built nothing in the project, and answers scenario by scenario. Its brief is fixed text: the agent that starts QA sends it as written, filling in only the project, the folder, the starting agent's name and model, and the commit to test.
“Auditors want proof of testing and approval.”Each release carries its QA result and its acceptance to main.

5

Working with AI agents

Seven conversations teams are having about building software with AI, and where this method answers them.

  • “AI writes faster than we can review.”

    What is reported
    A Harvard working paper by Fiona Chen and James Stratton, Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production, finds that after firms adopted coding agents there were more commits and more pull requests, the time from a pull request to its merge grew, and the rise in resolved issues was not statistically significant.
    What this method does
    Every feature arrives at code review with its scenarios and a recorded test run, so code review is not the first check. The strictest checking, QA, is spent only on what is chosen to ship.
    What stays true
    The method does not remove the cost of code review. That is why the rework each code review causes is watched and discussed with the maintainer.

  • “We are faster, but less stable.”

    What is reported
    Google's 2025 DORA report found that adopting AI now improves software delivery throughput and still increases delivery instability.
    What this method does
    The method holds work to two standards: fast into development, strict at stage. Instability is meant to be met at that gate, before a release, with each feature small and independent.

  • “Running agents in parallel just moves the conflicts to merge time.”

    What is reported
    Practitioners report that separate folders stop agents overwriting each other but do not prevent conflicts, that two agents told to work the backlog pick the same task, and that the person ends up as the coordination layer.
    What this method does
    Work is taken by assignment in the record, by name, one work item to a branch, so two agents do not take the same item, and the record is pushed whenever it changes so that every machine sees the claim. development is where conflicts are meant to surface. The record is the shared context the folders lack.

  • “The agent forgot what we decided.”

    What is reported
    Writers describe specifications going stale while the real state lives in someone's head, and recommend decision logs and handoff documents.
    What this method does
    The record is kept as the work happens, decisions are recorded in the turn they are made, and an agent's session starts by reading it. It also travels with the code, which a handoff document does not.

  • “Who wrote this, and can we prove it?”

    What is reported
    There are new tools for attributing lines to an AI, and no accepted standard yet for naming one in a commit.
    What this method does
    Every commit names the contributor, the agent, the model and the session. The person directing the work is its author, whatever share the agent typed.

  • “The specifications and tickets live somewhere the agent cannot see.”

    What is reported
    Anthropic's AI-native SDLC playbook recommends keeping the chain of artifacts in the product's repository, beside the code derived from it, as plain files that a person and an agent can both read and act on, with each stage committing something the next stage reads. It allows tickets and approvals to stay in an outside system, provided one source of truth is named.
    What this method does
    The record is that chain, in the repository: use cases, stories, scenarios, work items, decisions, attempts and test runs. It reaches every feature through the record branch, so whoever picks up the work, person or agent, already holds everything it rests on.
    Where this goes further
    The method goes further than the playbook in two places. The tickets themselves are in the repository, not linked from outside it. And decisions are kept as records of their own, in the words of whoever made them, where the playbook leaves them to merges and review approvals.

  • “We are drowning in low-quality AI contributions.”

    What is reported
    Open-source maintainers are adopting policies on AI-assisted contributions. The measures in use include disclosure of AI use, evidence that a change was built and tested, and, on some projects, accepting an AI-assisted change only for an issue already accepted.
    What this method does
    All three are this method's defaults: work starts from a work item, attribution is on every commit, and test runs are recorded. Small changes are its aim, and nothing enforces them.

Each source was opened and read by November 22, 2026, except where the list of sources says otherwise. The Harvard paper has been revised and its figures have changed between versions, so none is quoted here. Every source is listed under Sources.

sections.title: The road from the record to main
sections.html:
6

The road from the record to main

Work starts in the record and ends on main. A feature is code reviewed on its own branch, merged into development to be tested with the others, and merged into stage only when it is chosen for a release.
text: Work starts in the record and ends on `main`. A feature is code reviewed on its own branch, merged into `development` to be tested with the others, and merged into `stage` only when it is chosen for a release.
Figure: One feature travels from the record, through development and stage, to main; a second feature stays on development.

Step 1 of 10: The work is readied on the record: its work item, and its story and scenarios where it is new behaviour, are written and committed there. The work item names its scenarios or says why it has none. Until then it is still backlog and has no branch.
Step 2 of 10: A branch is cut from the record and named from its work item. A second feature is cut the same way. Neither holds anything of the other.

Step 3 of 10: Feature A's own tests pass in its own folder. Then its code is reviewed on its own branch by an agent that did not write it, and each finding is answered, before the feature goes anywhere. The test run and the code review are recorded, and the feature pulls the record, so it carries them onward.

Step 4 of 10: Each feature, code reviewed on its own branch, is merged into development by its own pull request, once, and they are tested together. Being on development does not mean a feature will be released.

Step 5 of 10: The maintainer chooses feature A for the release. The chosen set is first built and tested as a candidate on a machine, which a later section shows. Then feature A is merged into stage from its own branch, so it arrives without feature B.

Step 6 of 10: QA: the project's whole suite is run on stage itself, by a fresh agent that has built nothing in the project. It answers for each scenario and records its own run in the record, so the record says who ran it. It fixes nothing and pushes nothing.

Step 7 of 10: The maintainer accepts the release, which is the word to promote. QA has already recorded its own run, against the commit it tested. The acceptance is recorded in the maintainer's words, and the record is merged into stage by one more pull request, so the release carries both to main. A check confirms that nothing but the record changed on stage since the commit QA tested.

Step 8 of 10: On that same word, the agent that assembled stage promotes it to main by pull request and tags the release twice: a name of version, pull request and date for people, and the bare version for tools.

Step 9 of 10: The record pulls main. It is again main plus everything recorded since, and the next feature is cut from there. development and stage usually stay as they are: stage already holds what main holds, and the released feature is already on development.
Step 10 of 10: The record, now holding the release, is merged into development by pull request. This joins development to what was released; the section on resolving a conflict says why that matters.
Time runs left to right. Feature A is released. Feature B is tested on `development` and waits for a later release. No feature is ever cut from `development` or `stage`, and nothing pulls from them.

sections.title: What makes a feature eligible for stage
sections.html:
9

What makes a feature eligible for stage

Being on development is not enough. These six conditions are the bar for stage. A feature below it is chosen only by the maintainer's recorded decision.

  • Its scenarios pass

    Its work item names its scenarios, or says why it has none, and every scenario it names has a passing result recorded from the feature's own folder, for the code as it stands. A result made before the code last changed does not count; a pull of the record afterwards does not make it stale. A work item that names none must say why; silence does not meet this. For a member of a coordination, a passing result from the coordination branch's folder stands in its place when it is recorded on the member's work item, names the commit of each member, and no member has changed since.

  • Its code is reviewed

    By an agent that did not write it, with each finding dealt with as its kind requires. A finding put to the maintainer keeps the feature out until it is answered, and the answer, to fix it or to accept it as it is, is recorded.

  • It has pulled the record

    It has pulled the record since the last release, and after its own test run and code review were recorded, so it carries them.

  • It stands alone

    It holds no other unreleased feature's commits. A member of a coordination is chosen only with, or after, the members it requires.

  • No open defect

    None is recorded against it.

  • Its decisions are accepted, and its story agreed

    Every decision it rests on is accepted by the product owner, not still proposed. Any story an agent wrote for it has been seen and agreed by the product owner: a feature built from a story an agent wrote itself may be built to development, and waits at stage until then.

The release set is the maintainer's choice. The agent assembling the release says which features are eligible and why, from the record, and lists what each lacks. That agent may have built part of the set, so the fresh QA agent confirms its list against the record. If the maintainer includes one below the bar, that is recorded as the maintainer's decision, with what the feature lacked, and QA reports those scenarios as not verified.

- `development`: the released code; the record the features brought; + the record, merged in after each release and hotfix; + the code of every feature being tested
- `stage`: the released code; the record the features brought; + the code of the release set; + the record, merged in before promotion
`development`, `stage` and `docket-record` are permanent branches, created from `main` when the project starts. The branches are not environments, though in a project they may map to them.

sections.title: A release
sections.html:
12

A release

The same road, for a set of three features. A release is assembled on stage from the features chosen for it, verified there, and promoted to main as a whole, carrying its own QA result and acceptance.
text: The same road, for a set of three features. A release is assembled on `stage` from the features chosen for it, verified there, and promoted to `main` as a whole, carrying its own QA result and acceptance.

Figure: Three features are each code reviewed on their own branch, then tested together. Two are chosen for the release, verified on stage, and promoted to main with the record. Afterwards the record pulls main and the feature left out pulls the record; development and stage usually stay as they are.

Step 1 of 8: Each of three features passes its own tests in its own folder and is code reviewed on its own branch, with the findings answered. Then each is merged into development by its own pull request, once, and they are tested together. development may be broken; that is what it is there to find.

Step 2 of 8: The maintainer chooses A and C for the release. The set is first built as a candidate on a machine and the whole suite is run on it, which a later section shows. Then each is merged into stage from its own branch, in the same order, one pull request each. B is left out.

Step 3 of 8: QA: the project's whole suite is run on stage itself, by a fresh agent that has built nothing in the project. It answers for each scenario and records its own run in the record, so the record says who ran it. It fixes nothing and pushes nothing. A pass on development proves nothing about the release.

Step 4 of 8: The maintainer accepts the release, which is the word to promote. QA has already recorded its own run, against the commit it tested. The acceptance is recorded in the maintainer's words, and the record is merged into stage by one more pull request, so the release carries both to main. A check confirms that nothing but the record changed on stage since the commit QA tested.

Step 5 of 8: On that same word, the agent that assembled stage promotes it to main by pull request and tags the release twice: a name of version, pull request and date for people, and the bare version for tools.
Step 6 of 8: The record pulls main, so the record branch holds the release.
Step 7 of 8: The record, now holding the release, is merged into development by pull request. This joins development to what was released; the section on resolving a conflict says why that matters.

Step 8 of 8: Feature B, still in progress, pulls the record. It is already on development and stays there. development and stage usually stay as they are after a release: stage holds what main holds, and the released features are already on development.

After the release the record pulls `main`, goes into `development` by pull request, and each feature still in progress pulls the record. `development` and `stage` usually stay as they are: `stage` already holds what `main` holds, and the released features are already on `development`. The pull request from the record is what joins `development` to the release.

sections.title: The whole cycle, as a loop
sections.html:
13

The whole cycle, as a loop

The same release, drawn as rings. Time runs clockwise from the top, and one turn is one release. Where the linear picture ends, this one begins again.
text: The same release, drawn as rings. Time runs clockwise from the top, and one turn is one release. Where the linear picture ends, this one begins again.

Figure: One release drawn as a loop: a feature is cut from the record, code reviewed on its own branch, tested on development, chosen for stage, verified, and promoted to main with the record; the record pulls main and goes into development, features in progress pull the record, and the next turn begins. Development and stage usually stay as they are after a release.
Step 1 of 9: Work is readied on the record, and a feature is cut from it, named from its work item.

Step 2 of 9: Its own tests pass in its own folder, and its code is reviewed on its own branch, with each finding answered. Then it is merged into development, once, and tested together with the others.
Step 3 of 9: The maintainer chooses the release set. It is first built and tested as a candidate on a machine. Then each feature is merged into stage from its own branch, in the same order.

Step 4 of 9: QA: the project's whole suite is run on stage itself, by a fresh agent that has built nothing in the project. It answers for each scenario and records its own run in the record, so the record says who ran it. It fixes nothing and pushes nothing.

Step 5 of 9: The maintainer accepts the release, which is the word to promote. QA has already recorded its own run, against the commit it tested. The acceptance is recorded in the maintainer's words, and the record is merged into stage by one more pull request, so the release carries both to main. A check confirms that nothing but the record changed on stage since the commit QA tested.

Step 6 of 9: On that same word, the agent that assembled stage promotes it to main by pull request and tags the release twice: a name of version, pull request and date for people, and the bare version for tools.
Step 7 of 9: The record pulls main, so it is again main plus everything recorded since.
Step 8 of 9: The record, now holding the release, is merged into development by pull request. This joins development to what was released; the section on resolving a conflict says why that matters.

Step 9 of 9: Features still in progress pull the record. A feature that waits is already on development and goes round again. development and stage usually stay as they are after a release, and the next turn begins.
The rings are the branches, with `main` at the centre. A feature that is released ends when it reaches `stage`. A feature that waits goes all the way round, and an ordinary release breaks no ring.

sections.title: Testing the release set before stage is built
sections.html:
14

Testing the release set before stage is built

The features tried together on development are everything in progress, not the release set. So the chosen set is first built as a candidate on a machine: main plus the set, merged in release order and never pushed, with the whole suite run on the assembled set. The same features are then merged into stage in the same order, and stage is checked against the candidate.
text: The features tried together on `development` are everything in progress, not the release set. So the chosen set is first built as a candidate on a machine: `main` plus the set, merged in release order and never pushed, with the whole suite run on the assembled set. The same features are then merged into `stage` in the same order, and `stage` is checked against the candidate.
Figure: A candidate is built on a machine from main plus the release set and the suite is run on it. Stage is then built from the same features in the same order, and the two are compared.

Step 1 of 4: The maintainer has chosen the set, and each feature of it has pulled the record and been pushed. A candidate is built on a machine, in a folder of its own: main as it is on GitHub, plus the set, merged in release order. It is never pushed. A conflict between two features is resolved in the merge, and the merge resolves nothing else, so the same resolution is replayed when the set is merged into stage.

Step 2 of 4: The project's whole suite is run on the candidate: on the assembled set, not after each merge, and again whenever the set changes. A feature that breaks the set is left out, or fixed on its own branch, code reviewed there and merged into development again. The candidate is then built again, as many times as it takes, which costs nothing on GitHub.
Step 3 of 4: stage is built: the same features, merged one by one in the same order, each by its own pull request.

Step 4 of 4: stage is checked against the candidate, tree against tree. The merge commits differ; if the trees are identical, the pass on the candidate is evidence about what stage holds. QA on stage is its independent confirmation.

A break is found before `stage` exists, where leaving a feature out costs nothing on GitHub. Where people need to see the candidate running, it can be built on `development` instead. That is a case of items coming out of it: `development` is reset to `main` on the maintainer's word and the set is merged into it, so the candidate can be seen running wherever `development` is deployed. The features left out are merged into it again afterwards.

sections.title: How the history says where work is, and how a release is named
sections.html:
15

How the history says where work is, and how a release is named

A commit does not record its branch, but a merge's title names the branch merged and the branch merged into, and its body names the pull request that made it. Read by first parent, each permanent branch is one line per arrival.

A release's name is its tag: v<version>-pr<number>-<date>. The version comes first, then the number of the pull request that promoted stage to main, then the date of the promotion. A second tag on the same commit is the bare version, v<version>, for tools: under semantic versioning a hyphen after a version marks a pre-release, so a tool would rank the descriptive name below the release it names. Every merge made by pull request carries one line in its body, Pull-request: and the pull request's URL, so the merge commit itself leads to GitHub. Nothing is entered for the history of releases: it is read from the tags, the work items, QA's run and the acceptance.

Where a work item stands is read from the merges, not set by hand. Which of development, stage and main hold its branch is a fact of the history, and a status that says otherwise is wrong.

sections.title: Rework after a code review
sections.html:
16

Rework after a code review

A feature is code reviewed on its own branch, and its findings answered, before it is first merged into development, so that it is merged once. The builder classifies each finding and deals with it by its kind, and anything to fix is fixed where the feature was built.

Kind of findingWhat it isWhat happens to it
DefectThe code does not do what a scenario or a stated requirement says.Fixed on the feature's own branch.
RiskThe tests pass, but a wrong thing can happen: lost data, a race, an unsafe command.Fixed, or put to the maintainer to accept as it is.
Missing or weak testA scenario, or part of one, that no test really checks.Fixed where the scenario is otherwise unverified; otherwise recorded, for QA to report.
Untrue wordingA document, a message or a comment that says something untrue.Fixed. It never holds a feature back on its own.
Design or styleA preference about how the code is shaped, with no defect or risk in it.Recorded as a backlog item. It never holds a feature back.
WrongThe finding misreads the code or a convention of the repository.Rejected with the evidence. A tie-breaker confirms it: any agent that neither wrote the code nor raised the finding, given the finding and the evidence. It is then listed for the maintainer with its reason, and the work moves on; it is not asked.

The builder classifies each finding; the reviewer's own label, blocking or not, is not the classification. A finding put to the maintainer keeps the feature out of stage until it is answered, and the answer, to fix it or to accept it as it is, is recorded. The reviewer first reads what is already settled, the project's decisions and the code review records of earlier features, so a finding already rejected is not raised again unless something has changed.

Figure: A feature is code reviewed on its own branch before its first merge. Each finding is classified and dealt with by its kind. A defect or a risk is fixed on the feature's own branch and the fix is code reviewed. The feature is then merged into development once, and on stage it gets QA only.

Step 1 of 6: The feature is built and its own tests pass in its own folder. Before it is merged anywhere, its code is reviewed on its own branch by an agent that did not write it. The code review reads the feature's own code and tests, and reports findings.

Step 2 of 6: The builder classifies each finding, and acts on its kind: a defect, a risk, a missing or weak test, untrue wording, design or style, or wrong. The reviewer's own label, blocking or not, is not the classification. The table below says what happens to each kind.

Step 3 of 6: A defect, and a risk that is not put to the maintainer, is fixed on the feature's own branch. Where the feature's attempt has already ended, the work item goes back to active and gets a new attempt for the rework, with an estimate, naming the findings. Any agent may take it, by assignment.

Step 4 of 6: The rework is code reviewed again only when it fixed a defect or a risk. That code review reads whether the fix closes the finding, and what the fix itself changed; it is not a second reading of the feature. Rework for a test, for wording or for a backlog item is not code reviewed again.

Step 5 of 6: The code review is recorded beside the work item: the decision, and each finding with its kind and how it ended. The feature pulls the record and is merged into development by pull request, once, and tested with the others.

Step 6 of 6: When it is chosen, it is merged into stage from its own branch. Nothing is code reviewed on stage: each feature's code review was done once, at the feature, and stage gets QA only, by a fresh agent.

A feature that was already on `development` when it was reworked is merged into it again by pull request; `development` is not reset for it. How much rework each code review caused is said, and discussed with the user.

sections.title: When a feature fails on stage
sections.html:
17

When a feature fails on stage

If stage fails, it is not left standing, and a candidate with a known defect is never offered for promotion. A failed feature is not backed out. Usually it comes out, and stage is rebuilt without it; where the fault is small and quickly fixed on the feature's own branch, the feature may be merged again on top. Either way stage is checked again.

When to reset development or stage, and when to leave it running

Both can be reset to main when that serves the work. This is guidance, not a list to apply by rote: say which case you see and why, and where it is not plain, ask. A reset is a push, so it is on the maintainer's word; the word to build a release candidate covers the resets of stage that the candidate needs. The record branch is never reset.

A reset is usually right

  • Something has to come out

    A feature on development is abandoned or broken and holding the others up; a feature has failed on stage.

  • A clean start is needed

    Before a hotfix, stage is reset so that the fix travels alone. Before a release set is assembled, stage is reset if it holds anything main does not.

  • The branch is to show one thing

    development is rebuilt from a release set so that people can see that candidate running.

  • The branch can no longer be trusted

    It has taken a merge it should not have, or so much has gone wrong on it that finding the cause costs more than building it again.

It is usually better left running

  • After an ordinary release or hotfix

    stage already holds what main holds, and the released features are already on development; the record going into development joins it to the release.

  • While features on it are still being tried together

    Resetting development means merging each of them again.

  • When a small correction to a feature of the set is quicker and as safe

    The feature is fixed on its own branch and merged again by pull request, on top of what is there, where rebuilding the whole set would cost more than it protects. Nothing is ever changed on the branch itself.

After a reset, the features that should still be there are merged again, each from its own branch by pull request, and everyone is told, so that anyone with a copy takes it from GitHub again.

Usually it comes out, and `stage` is rebuilt without it; where the fault is small and quickly fixed on the feature's own branch, the feature may be merged again on top. Either way `stage` is checked again.

Figure: Three features are merged into stage and one fails. Stage is not left standing. Usually the feature comes out: stage is reset to main, the candidate is built again from the other two, they are merged again, and stage is verified again.
Step 1 of 5: The release set, already tested together as a candidate, is merged into stage, one pull request for each feature.
Step 2 of 5: Feature C fails when stage is verified. stage is not left standing with a known fault. The failure is recorded against feature C, with the step that caught it and its kind.

Step 3 of 5: Usually the feature comes out, as drawn here: stage is reset to main. This does not wait for a separate word. The failed feature is not backed out, and nothing is patched on stage. Where the fault is small and the feature is fixed quickly on its own branch, it may be merged again on top by pull request, and stage is not reset.

Step 4 of 5: The candidate is built again from A and B, and the whole suite is run on it. Then A and B are merged into stage again from their own branches, in the same order, and stage is checked against the candidate.

sections.title: When items need to come out of development
sections.html:
18

When items need to come out of development

This is the usual reason to reset development; the cases are listed in the section before. After an ordinary release it usually stays as it is. Rebuilding it from a release set, to test that set as a candidate, is a case of the same thing: everything outside the set comes out, and is merged in again afterwards.
text: This is the usual reason to reset `development`; the cases are listed in the section before. After an ordinary release it usually stays as it is. Rebuilding it from a release set, to test that set as a candidate, is a case of the same thing: everything outside the set comes out, and is merged in again afterwards.
Figure: Development is reset to main when an item needs to come out of it. The features still in progress are then merged into it again from their own branches.
Step 1 of 3: Feature C needs to come out of development. An ordinary release does not cause this: after a release the released features are already on development, so it is usually left as it is.
Step 2 of 3: On the maintainer's word, development is reset to main. Everyone is told, so that anyone with a copy takes it from GitHub again.

Step 3 of 3: Every feature it held that is still in progress and does not need to come out is merged into it again, each from its own branch by pull request. Recorded resolutions replay a conflict already resolved on that machine.
When `development` is reset, every surviving feature is merged again, so the same conflict can come up again. Git's recorded resolutions replay it.

sections.title: A hotfix
sections.html:
19

A hotfix

A hotfix is a fix that cannot wait for the next release. It takes a release's road from stage onward, alone. It does not pass through development, and it never goes straight to main.
text: A hotfix is a fix that cannot wait for the next release. It takes a release's road from `stage` onward, alone. It does not pass through `development`, and it never goes straight to `main`.
Figure: An incident is recorded, a hotfix is cut from the record, stage is reset, and the hotfix is released alone through stage to main. Development then gets the fix from the record.
Step 1 of 8: The record pulls main, so it is up to what is released.
Step 2 of 8: The incident is recorded on the record, as a work item of the incident kind, and committed. The decision to make a hotfix is itself recorded.
Step 3 of 8: The hotfix is cut from the record and named from the incident. It is a branch from what is released that already holds its own record.
Step 4 of 8: stage is reset to main. A release that was being assembled there is set aside, and is merged into stage again once the hotfix is out.
Step 5 of 8: The fix is made and tested, the record is pulled, and the fix's code is reviewed by an agent that did not write it. Then it is merged into stage by pull request.

Step 6 of 8: stage is verified by a fresh agent; the set is the one fix, so there is no candidate to build first. If it fails, the fix is corrected on the hotfix branch and code reviewed there, stage is reset to main again, and the fix is merged and checked again. Then the record is brought into stage, and it is promoted to main and tagged, on the maintainer's word. The hotfix never goes straight to main.
Step 7 of 8: As after any release, the record pulls main, and every feature in progress pulls the record. stage already holds what main holds.

Step 8 of 8: development does not hold the fix. It gets it from the record, which now holds it, by pull request. This is the same step as after any release. development need not be reset for a hotfix, and the features on it stay where they are.

The incident is recorded before the branch exists, so the hotfix holds its own record from its first commit. Afterwards `development` gets the fix from the record by pull request. If the fix conflicts with a feature there, the conflict shows in that pull request.

sections.title: A bad release already on main
sections.html:
20

A bad release already on main

Rolling back is two things, in this order: put production back, then correct the release. main is never reverted or rewritten.
text: Rolling back is two things, in this order: put production back, then correct the release. `main` is never reverted or rewritten.
Figure: A bad release already on main is put back by deploying the previous release again, which changes nothing in Git, and is then corrected by a hotfix that goes through stage like any other.
Step 1 of 4: A release turns out to be bad after it is promoted and deployed.

Step 2 of 4: Production is put back first. The previous release is deployed again, from its tag, on the maintainer's word. This is a deployment and changes nothing in Git: main is not rewritten, and no tag is moved or deleted.
Step 3 of 4: The bad release is then corrected by the hotfix road. The incident is recorded, and the hotfix is cut from the record. The fix may do no more than undo the bad change.

Step 4 of 4: The hotfix goes through stage, is verified and is promoted like any other, and the corrected release is deployed. Nothing is reverted on main directly, and the bad release keeps its tag and its record.

Putting production back is a deployment and changes nothing in Git. The stage reset, the record going into `stage` and the steps after a release are as in the hotfix above and are left out of this drawing.

sections.title: Resolving a conflict
sections.html:
21

Resolving a conflict

Whoever opened the pull request resolves the conflict. Nothing is pushed to development or stage to get round one.

A merge resolves its conflict and nothing else. Any other change features need in order to work together is written on a feature's own branch, never in a merge and never on development or stage, and the feature is merged again. Where such a change is only right with the other features present, those features require each other, and the answer is a coordination.

A conflict GitHub reports and Git does not have. A branch cut from the record holds every released feature, because the record has pulled main. development holds the same features by another route, its own pull requests. Until the two are joined they share each released feature separately, and GitHub reports a conflict on a pull request that Git on a machine merges cleanly. The cure is the join made after every release and hotfix: the record goes into development by pull request. If the merge branch has become routine, something is unjoined, and that is what to say.
text: Whoever opened the pull request resolves the conflict. Nothing is pushed to `development` or `stage` to get round one.

Figure: A pull request that does not merge is resolved on a merge branch cut from the receiving branch. The feature is merged into it, the conflict is resolved there, and the pull request is opened from that branch.
Step 1 of 4: The feature's pull request into development does not merge. Whoever opened it resolves the conflict.
Step 2 of 4: A merge branch is cut from development as it is on GitHub.
Step 3 of 4: The feature is merged into the merge branch, and the conflict is resolved in that merge. The merge resolves the conflict and nothing else. The feature itself is not changed.
Step 4 of 4: The pull request is opened from the merge branch and merged. With recorded resolutions turned on, Git replays the resolution if the same conflict comes up on stage or after a reset.

The same means serves `stage`. The merge is made on a machine, so Git's reuse of recorded resolutions (rerere, turned on once per clone with `git config rerere.enabled true`) applies: the same conflict, resolved once, is replayed when it comes up again on that machine. The recordings are kept per clone, and sharing them between people and agents is not arranged yet. A merge branch is for a real conflict, and it is the one branch ever cut from `development` or `stage`.

A merge resolves its conflict and nothing else. Any other change features need in order to work together is written on a feature's own branch, never in a merge and never on `development` or `stage`, and the feature is merged again. Where such a change is only right with the other features present, those features require each other, and the answer is a coordination.

A conflict GitHub reports and Git does not have. A branch cut from the record holds every released feature, because the record has pulled `main`. `development` holds the same features by another route, its own pull requests. Until the two are joined they share each released feature separately, and GitHub reports a conflict on a pull request that Git on a machine merges cleanly. The cure is the join made after every release and hotfix: the record goes into `development` by pull request. If the merge branch has become routine, something is unjoined, and that is what to say.

Features that require each other

sections.title: Why every branch is cut from the record
sections.html:
23

Why every branch is cut from the record

Git can merge a branch into any branch it shares an ancestor with. What the branch was cut from decides what comes with it. This is the rule the rest of the method rests on, and the first thing not to do.
text: Git can merge a branch into any branch it shares an ancestor with. What the branch was cut from decides what comes with it. This is the rule the rest of the method rests on, and the first thing not to do.
Figure: A feature cut from development carries every other feature into stage with it. A feature cut from the record arrives on stage alone.

Features A and B are already on `development`. Cut from there, feature X carries both into `stage`. Cut from the record, which holds no unreleased code, it arrives alone and can be chosen for a release by itself. The other ways to end up carrying work that was not chosen are in the next section.

sections.title: The other mistakes, in pairs
sections.html:
24

The other mistakes, in pairs

Cutting from development, above, is the plainest case. Each of these does the same kind of damage by another route: it looks harmless when it is done and costs a release later. Wrong on the left, right on the right.

  • Don't Commit code on the record branch, or change the record on a feature.

    Do The record is changed on the record branch, through Docket, and a feature pulls it.

  • Don't Commit on development or stage, or merge into either on your own machine.

    Do Both change only by a pull request on GitHub, merged as a real merge.

  • Don't Cut a branch for work that is not ready.

    Do Its work item, and its story and scenarios where it is new behaviour, are committed on the record first. A work item with no scenario and no reason for having none is not ready. A fix names the scenario it restores, or adds one for the fault. A standing instruction to keep working does not change this.

  • Don't Change anything in a merge beyond its conflict.

    Do A merge resolves its conflict and nothing else. Any other change features need in order to work together is written on a feature's own branch, and the feature is merged again. Where the change is only right with the other features present, they are tied in a coordination.

  • Don't Merge a feature into development before its code review.

    Do It is code reviewed on its own branch, and the findings answered, first, so that it is merged once.

  • Don't Commit work on a coordination branch, or merge it anywhere.

    Do The work is done on the member's own branch, and the member is merged into the coordination branch again. The members go onward one by one.

  • Don't Reset development or stage by rote.

    Do Both can be reset to main when that serves the work. Say which case you see and why, and where it is not plain, ask. After an ordinary release both usually stay as they are: the released features are already on development.

  • Don't Leave stage standing with a known fault.

    Do Usually the feature comes out and stage is reset. Where the fault is small and quickly fixed on the feature's own branch, it may be merged again on top. Either way stage is checked again.

  • Don't Count a scenario as passed because the suite passed.

    Do QA answers for each scenario, and reports one with no test as no test found.
